See the "wisdom of this world", see the "wisdom of the princes of this world", how they reproach the "wisdom" of my Christ, how they reproach the "wisdom" of the true Judaism, according to which we are circumcised spiritually, while those others are cut off. Understand, then, how the "wisdom of this world and of the princes of this world" reviles "wisdom"; and on this account a "man" is sought who may be with these "seven" spiritual "women", that he may "take away their reproach". Properly there is "one" "man" who may "take away their reproach". Who is this "man"? Jesus, who "came forth according to the flesh" "from the root of Jesse", "made of the seed of David according to the flesh, predestined the Son of God in power according to the spirit of justification". For "there came forth a rod from the root of Jesse". The "rod" is not "the firstborn of all creation", the "rod" is not "he who in the beginning was with God, God the Word", but "a rod from the root of Jesse", who "was born according to the flesh". "There came forth", therefore, "a rod from the root of Jesse, and a flower ascended from his root". What is the "flower" and what is the "root"? For both are one in him who lies beneath; but the difference is one of dealings. For if you are a sinner, there is no "flower" for you, nor will you see the "flower which is from the root of Jesse"; for the "rod" will come even to you, just as the disciple speaks of the "rod" and the "flower". Of the "rod" indeed he says: "what do you wish? shall I come to you with a rod?", but of the "flower": "or in the love of God and the spirit of gentleness?". "There came forth", therefore, "from the root of Jesse a rod" for him who is punished with penalties, a "rod" for him who needs rebuke, a "rod" for him who has need to be reproved; but a "flower" for him who is already instructed and does not need harsh correction, or at least does not need punishments, but is now strong enough to begin to flower toward perfect fruit. For first the "flower" is shown, and then after the "flower" it becomes a "rod" unto fruit. "There came forth a rod from the root of Jesse, and a flower ascended from his root. And the seven women shall rest, the Spirit of God, the spirit of wisdom and understanding shall rest upon him". For the "spirit of wisdom" did "not rest" in Moses, the "spirit of wisdom" did "not rest" in Joshua son of Nun, the "spirit of wisdom" did "not rest" in each of the prophets, in Isaiah, in Jeremiah.

But do not stone me as though I were blaspheming, while I desire to glorify my Lord Jesus Christ; rather, bearing with me, consider what is said, and you will see that in none of them did the "spirit rest", not because it came to none, but because it "rested" in none. It came "upon" Moses, and Moses does not believe after the "spirit of wisdom" that came to him. For he says: "Hear, you rebels: shall I bring forth water for you out of this rock?" It came "upon" all the just, it came also "upon" Isaiah. But what does he say? "Having unclean lips, and I dwell in the midst of a people having unclean lips". The "spirit of wisdom" came after that "tongs" and fire, it came to him "having unclean lips", but it did "not rest". It used him indeed as a minister, but it did "not rest"; it is troubled, to whatever of men it comes. For every man sins, "there is no just man upon the earth who does good and does not sin"; "no one is clean from filth, not even if his life be of one day, but his months are numbered". Therefore it "rests upon" none. We can also prove from the Gospel that the "spirit came upon" many and "did not remain in" them. A little while ago it was read: "my spirit shall not remain in these men forever"; he does not say: it shall not be, but: "it shall not remain". John saw one alone in whom it "remained", and this was the sign: "upon whom you shall see the Spirit descending and remaining upon him, this is the Son of God". A certain one ministered to the Word of God when the "spirit descended"; a little after he "sins", a little after he speaks an "idle word". But I do not know whether he even remains without sin; do you think that, with the "spirit" present, it is granted to sin? "Upon" none, therefore, did "the Spirit of God rest", according to what is written: "there came forth a rod from the root of Jesse, and a flower ascended from his root, and the Spirit of God shall rest upon him, the spirit of wisdom, the spirit of understanding, the spirit of counsel and might". On account of this he is the "angel of great counsel", on account of this he grew strong and, growing strong, ascended, and the powers marvel at him as he ascends and say of him: this is "the Lord strong and mighty in battle". To him, then, as he ascends into the heavenly places, or to his strength, I will say that: "the spirit of counsel and might rested upon him"; "the Lord is my strength and my praise, and he has become for me salvation". "There rested", therefore, "upon him the Spirit of God, the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and might, the spirit of knowledge and piety, and the spirit of the fear of God filled him".

The "women", therefore, seeking whom they may "take, seven shall lay hold of one man". And this depends on what precedes, and one must first know when the "seven women receive one man". When the "strong ones" of Jerusalem "have been humbled", when the "cases of the ornament" of the daughters of Zion "have mourned", when she "has been left" "alone", when she "has been dashed to the ground", then "seven women shall lay hold of one man, saying: we will eat our own bread, and we will be clothed with our own garments; only let your name be invoked upon us", then "did they lay hold" and truly hold fast "seven women, one man", Jesus Christ our Lord, according to which he is understood to be "man", according to which he was born, according to which he took up a body. "Seven women shall lay hold of one man, saying: we will eat our own bread". Many "men" walk about and the "women lay hold" of none, no "man" pleases them; for it is not on account of a scarcity of men that they "lay hold of one man", but on account of the rarity of the "man" such as they wished, such as they sought; "one" "man" only they found, whom they "laid hold of", that they might "say" to him: "we will eat our own bread and be clothed with our own garments". There is a certain food of "wisdom", there is likewise a certain food both of "understanding" and of the other "spirits". What is this food? I am not afraid to say: there is another food beyond these; perhaps, as my food is the word of God, who says: "I am the living bread who came down from heaven" and "I give life to the world", so the food of "wisdom" is the Father himself, on account of this: "my food is to do the will of him who sent me, and to complete his work". Nor is it to be thought that "wisdom" and "understanding" and the rest of the "spirits" lack anything, because they have another food, since of the whole dispensation there is one food, the nature of God. "We will eat our own bread and be clothed with our own garments". There is a certain adornment of "wisdom", with which it is adorned; "wisdom" is adorned with speech. Each of these "women" has her adornments. "Only let your name be invoked upon us, take away our reproach". What is the "name of wisdom"? Jesus. What is: "let your name be invoked upon us"? I am "wisdom", I wish to be called by your name, that I, "wisdom", may be called Jesus, that "understanding" and "great counsel" and "might" and "knowledge" and "piety" and "the fear of God" may be named Jesus, that your "name" may become "all in all". "Let your name be invoked upon us, take away our reproach". Truly Jesus "took away the reproach". Therefore, rising up, let us pray to God, who sent this "man" and in whom "the spirit of the seven women rested", that this "man" may grant to us also the fellowship of these "women", and that, taking them up, we may become wise and understanding in God, and that the other virtues may adorn our soul in Christ Jesus, "to whom is glory and dominion unto the ages of ages, Amen!".

Isa.author: Origen of Alexandria
Isa.quote: Then there follows: "when the days of their purification were fulfilled, according to the law of Moses, they brought him to Jerusalem". On account of the purification, he says, "of them". Of whom, "of them"? If it had been written: on account of her purification, that is, of Mary, who had given birth, no question would arise, and we would boldly say that Mary, who was human, had need of purification after childbirth. But now, in that it says: "the days of their purification", it seems to signify not one, but another or several. Did Jesus, then, have need of purification and was he unclean, or defiled with some filth? Perhaps I seem to speak rashly, but I am moved by the authority of the Scriptures. See what is written in Job: "no one is clean from filth, not even if his life should be of a single day". He did not say: "no one is clean from sin," but: "no one is clean from filth". For filth and sins do not signify the same thing; and that you may know that filth means one thing and sin another, Isaiah teaches most plainly, saying: "the Lord will wash away the filth of the sons and daughters of Zion, and will cleanse the blood from their midst, by the spirit of judgment the filth and by the spirit of burning the blood". Every soul that has been clothed with a human body has its own "filth". And that you may know that Jesus too was made filthy by his own will, because for our salvation he had assumed a human body, listen to the prophet Zechariah saying: "Jesus was clothed with filthy garments".
Isa.source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 14

Isa.author: Origen of Alexandria
Isa.quote: When one has recognized the differences in sins, one can see how the Lord says in Isaiah, "The Lord will wash away the filth of the sons and daughters of Zion and will cleanse the blood from their midst by a spirit of judgment and a spirit of burning." Filth is washed away by a spirit of judgment. Blood is washed away by a spirit of burning. Even if you have not committed a sin that leads to death, you have still sinned and have thereby become filthy. The Lord will wash away the filth of the sons and daughters of Zion, and he will cleanse the blood from among them. A spirit of judgment will be the recompense for filth, and a spirit of burning will be a recompense for the blood. Whenever we commit heinous sins, we do not need lye or washing with soap; rather we need the spirit of burning.

Isa.author: Origen of Alexandria
Isa.quote: But hear what the prophet says: "By your sins you were sold, and for your iniquities I dismissed your mother." You see, then, that we are indeed all the creature of God, but each one is sold by his own sins and for his own iniquities departs from his own creator. We are, therefore, God's, according as we were created by him; but we became slaves of the devil, according as we were sold by our sins. But Christ, coming, "redeemed us," while we were serving that lord to whom we had sold our very selves by sinning. And so he seems to have received back as his own those whom he had created, but to have acquired as aliens those who by sinning had sought for themselves an alien lord.

Isa.author: Origen of Alexandria
Isa.quote: If then this is the character of the body that rises from the dead, let us now see what is the meaning of the threatened "eternal fire." Now we find in the prophet Isaiah that the fire by which each person is punished is described as belonging to himself. For it says, "Walk in the light of your fire and in the flame which you have kindled for yourselves." These words seem to indicate that every sinner kindles for himself the flame of his own fire and is not plunged into a fire that has been previously kindled by someone else or that existed before him.

Isa.author: Origen of Alexandria
Isa.quote: That "fire" is not "from the altar". The fire which is "from the altar" is the fire of the Lord; but that which is outside the altar is not the Lord's, but is the proper fire of each one of those who sin, of which it is said: "their worm shall not die, and their fire shall not be extinguished". That "fire" therefore is of those very ones who kindled it, as also elsewhere it is written: "walk in your fire and in the flame which you have kindled for yourselves". But to Isaiah not his own fire is applied, but the fire of the altar, which will "purge around" his "lips".

Isa.author: Origen of Alexandria
Isa.quote:
They were ignorant of the words of the prophet Isaiah, who prophesied these very same things concerning him, and said in the person of the Lord and Savior himself: "what, that I came, and there was no man? I called, and there was none who would obey? Is my hand not able to rescue? Or can I not deliver? Behold, at my rebuke I will make the sea a desert, and I will set the rivers a desert. And their fish shall be dried up because they have no water, and shall die of thirst. And I will clothe the heaven with darkness, and make its covering like sackcloth. The Lord gives me the tongue of instruction, that I may know how it behooves me to speak the word; he set me in the morning, he applied to me an ear to hear, and the instruction of the Lord shall open my ears; but I am not unbelieving, nor do I contradict. I offered my back to the scourges, and my cheeks to the palms of hands, but I did not turn away my face from the confusion of spittings, and the Lord God became my helper". For all who are of the Church confess him to be Christ who says: "the Lord, the Lord gave me the tongue of instruction" and the rest which I have expounded.

But I have fittingly expounded also those things which above were joined to these, wishing to show that this was prophesied concerning that glorious one, that he should be spat upon and buffeted. For to what other does it fit to say: "I came", except to Christ who came into the world? Or whom did it befit to say: "I called, and there was none who would obey", except him who came to call the people of the Jews and was not heard, and therefore did not rescue the people nor deliver it, but forsook it? And it is Christ who says: "behold, at my rebuke I will make the sea a desert, and I will set the rivers a desert", who is to bring about the consummation of the world. For it is he who will clothe the heaven with "darkness" and clothe it "as with sackcloth", and, receiving from the Father the "tongue of instruction", knew how "it behooved him to speak the word" which God had entrusted to him; and "he applied to him an ear", that he might hear more than all who hear, and the "instruction" of the Father opened his ear, because he was not unbelieving to the Father who sent him nor contradicting, and by the very deed he taught those desiring to learn meekness and praiseworthy humility. And there was a work in this, that he taught these things by deeds, offering his "back to the scourges and his cheeks to the palms of hands" and not turning away his face "from the confusion of spittings", so that us (as I judge), who had all been worthy to suffer these disgraces, he himself might rescue by suffering them for us. For he did "not die for us", that we might not die, but that we might not die for ourselves; and he was struck with blows for us and was spat upon, so that we, who had been worthy of all these things on account of our sins, might not suffer them, but that, suffering them for righteousness, we might receive them gladly.

Isa.author: Origen of Alexandria
Isa.quote: "Be separated", indeed, "you who carry the vessels of the Lord, and go out from the midst of them, says the Lord". "Separate yourself" from earthly deeds, "separate yourself" from the concupiscence of the world: "for everything that is in the world", according to the Apostle, "is the concupiscence of the flesh and the concupiscence of the eyes, which is not from God". When therefore you have separated yourself from all these things, devote yourself to God as a firstborn calf; let sin not work through you, nor let malice impose a yoke upon you, but be set aside and set apart, given over only to priestly uses like a firstborn animal.… But we say that one is set apart not by places, but by deeds, and not by regions, but by manners of life. Finally, the very word which in the Greek language is spoken, ἅγιος, signifies as it were to be outside the earth. For whoever shall have consecrated himself to God will rightly be seen to be outside the earth and outside the world; for he too is able to say, walking upon the earth: "we have our manner of life in the heavens".

Isa.author: Origen of Alexandria
Isa.quote: "How are beautiful are the feet of those who announce good things!" Since Isaiah perceived the beautiful and opportune preaching of the apostles who follow the One who said, "I am the way," he praises the feet that proceed over the intelligible way, which is Christ Jesus, and go in to God through the door. Those whose feet are beautiful announce Jesus as "good tidings."
Isa.source_title: COMMENTARY ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN 1:11

Isa.author: Origen of Alexandria
Isa.quote: There are, indeed, admitted to be recorded some statements respecting the body of Jesus having been "ill-favored"; not, however, "ignoble," as has been stated, nor is there any certain evidence that he was "little."

Isa.author: Origen of Alexandria
Isa.quote: It is possible also in another way to see a twofold coming of Christ, that is, the coming of the Word into the soul. First indeed the untrained and those then beginning to know Christ, because they cannot see the brightness of his beauty, say: "we saw him, and he had no form nor comeliness, but his appearance was without honor". Now the unhonored appearance of the Word is the foolish preaching about Christ, when we preach Christ born and crucified. But the second coming is the coming of Christ among perfect men, concerning whom the steward of his word says: "but we speak wisdom among the perfect". And these perfect ones have become lovers of his beauty and beseech the Word, that he gird upon himself his rational sword and set it about the mystery of the fleshly nativity, which is called mystically the thigh. For disciples of this kind praise the beauty and comeliness of the Word, and to this second coming is joined the consummation of the age in the man coming to perfection and saying: "but far be it from me to glory, save in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world is crucified to me and I to the world".

Isa.author: Origen of Alexandria
Isa.quote: Now those who are saved are called sheep because of their meekness, which they learned from him who says: "learn from me, for I am gentle and humble of heart," and because "even unto slaughter" they were ready to come, imitating Christ, who "was led as a sheep to the slaughter, and as a lamb before the one shearing it, without voice" — and not simply "without voice," but "before the one shearing it, without voice," that is, before the one taking away what is his own and plundering it.

Isa.author: Origen of Alexandria
Isa.quote: So when he was not a desert or a land made dry to Israel, he was, with respect to what is particular, a desert and land made dry to the pagan nations. But when he turned away from Israel and became to that Israel like a desert and land made dry, then grace was poured forth on the pagan nations, and Jesus Christ became now to us not a desert but abundance, and not a land made dry but one that bears fruit.

Isa.author: Origen of Alexandria
Isa.quote: It seems to me also that that fancy of Plato, that those stones that we call precious stones which derive their luster from a reflection, as it were, of the stones in that better land, is taken from the words of Isaiah in describing the city of God: "I will make your battlements of jasper, your stones shall be crystal and your borders of precious stones."

Isa.author: Origen of Alexandria
Isa.quote: And truly he was "a horn of salvation in the house of David", because this prophecy is sung in harmony: "For a vineyard was made on a horn". On what horn? On Christ Jesus, on him of whom it is now written: "he raised up a horn of salvation for us, in the house of David his servant, as he spoke through the mouth of his holy prophets".
Isa.source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 10

Isa.author: Origen of Alexandria
Isa.quote: See then how very bad sinning is, that they may be delivered to Satan, who holds captive the souls of those forsaken by God—though God does not forsake without cause or judgment those whom he has abandoned. For when he sends the rain for the vineyard and the vineyard bears thorns instead of grapes, what else will God do except order the clouds not to sprinkle rain on the vineyard?

Isa.author: Origen of Alexandria
Isa.quote: See then how very bad sinning is, that they may be delivered to Satan, who holds captive the souls of those forsaken by God—though God does not forsake without cause or judgment those whom he has abandoned. For when he sends the rain for the vineyard and the vineyard bears thorns instead of grapes, what else will God do except order the clouds not to sprinkle rain on the vineyard?

Isa.author: Origen of Alexandria
Isa.quote: And the Logos, exhorting us to come to this light, says, in the prophecies of Isaiah, "Enlighten yourself, enlighten yourself, O Jerusalem, for your light is come, and the glory of the Lord is risen on you." Observe now the difference between the fine phrases of Plato respecting the chief good and the declarations of our prophets regarding the light of the blessed; and notice that the truth as it is contained in Plato concerning this subject did not at all help his readers to attain to a pure worship of God, or even himself, who could philosophize so grandly about the chief good, whereas the simple language of the Scriptures led to their honest readers being filled with a divine spirit; and this light is nourished within them by the oil, which as a certain parable is said to have preserved the light of the torches of the five wise virgins.

Isa.author: Origen of Alexandria
Isa.quote: And they will be called the city of the Lord, Zion of holy Israel. On account of your being trapped and despised when there was no help, I will give you eternal rejoicing and joy for ages to come. And though you desire the milk of the nations and to consume the riches of kings, so that you might know that I am the Lord who saved you and led you out of Israel, "I will render for you gold instead of brass, and silver instead of steel … and I will give you rulers in peace and your bishops in justice, and injustice will no longer be heard in your land."
Isa.source_title: COMMENTARY ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN 10:294

Isa.author: Origen of Alexandria
Isa.quote: We must keep in mind, however, that the Word promises to the righteous through the mouth of Isaiah that days will come when not the sun but the Lord will be to them an everlasting light, and God will be their glory. And it is from misunderstanding, I think, some pestilent heresy that gave an interpretation to the words "let there be light," as if they were the expression of a wish merely on the part of the Creator, that Celsus made the remark, "The Creator did not borrow light from above, like those persons who kindle lamps at those of their neighbors."

Isa.author: Origen of Alexandria
Isa.quote: Let us therefore contemplate what those things are which he spoke in the prophet and afterward sounds forth about himself in the synagogue. "He sent me", it says, "to evangelize the poor". The "poor" signifies the nations; for these were "poor", possessing nothing at all, not God, not the law, not the prophets, not justice and the remaining virtues. For which cause God sent him to announce to the poor: "to preach release to the captives". Captives we were, whom for so many years Satan had bound, holding us captive and subject to himself. Jesus came "to preach release to the captives and to the blind, that they might see"; for indeed by the word and preaching of his teaching the blind see. Let the preaching therefore be understood ἀπὸ κοινοῦ (in common), not only over the captives, but also over the blind. "To send forth the broken into liberty". What was ever so broken and crushed as man, who was released and healed by Jesus? "To preach the acceptable year of the Lord". According to the simple understanding they say that the Savior preached the Gospel in Judea for one year, and that this is what is said: "to preach the acceptable year of the Lord and the day of retribution", unless perhaps the divine word signifies something of a mystery in the preaching of the year of the Lord. For there are to be other days, not such as we now discern in the world, and other months, and a different order of the Kalends. Just therefore as those are other, so also the year of the Lord to come is pleasing. But all these things have been foretold, that after sight from blindness, after liberty from chains, after health from diverse wounds, we may come to the "acceptable year of the Lord".
Isa.source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 32

Isa.author: Origen of Alexandria
Isa.quote: Blessed is that soul which, by the gore of blood poured out in martyrdom, casts down the airy throngs of demons that meet it. Blessed is he of whom, as he goes to heaven, the angels speak that prophetic word: "Who is this that comes up from Bozrah?"—that is, who ascends from the flesh to heaven. "Who is this that comes up from Bozrah, the redness of his garments?"—by the "redness of his garments" signifying the gore of blood. Blessed, then, are the souls that so follow Christ as Christ went before them. And therefore, because they so follow, they arrive even at the very altar of God, where the Lord Jesus Christ Himself is, the "high priest of the good things to come," "to whom is glory and power unto the ages of ages. Amen!"

Isa.author: Origen of Alexandria
Isa.quote: If a person, because he is too tenacious of life or too weak in the face of suffering, or because of the apparently convincing arguments of such as seek to induce us to accept the evil choice, has denied the one and only God and his Christ and borne testimony to demons or goddesses of fortune, then this person must realize that in doing this he is "setting," as it were, "a table for the demon and offering libations" to Fortune, "forsaking the Lord" and "forgetting his holy mount." He will incur the reproaches written in Isaiah.

Isa.author: Origen of Alexandria
Isa.quote: Isaiah also, declaring prophetically that there will be a new heaven and a new earth, undoubtedly suggests a similar view. For this renewal of heaven and earth, and this transformation of the form of the present world and this changing of the heavens will undoubtedly be prepared for those who are walking along and are tending to that goal of happiness to which, it is said, even enemies themselves are to be subjected and in which God is said to be "all in all." And if anyone imagines that at the end, material, that is, bodily nature will be entirely destroyed, he cannot in any respect meet my view, how beings so numerous and powerful are able to live and to exist without bodies, since it is an attribute of the divine nature alone.… Another, perhaps, may say that in the end every bodily substance will be so pure and refined as to be like the ether and of a celestial purity and clearness. How things will be, however, is known with certainty to God alone and to those who are his friends through Christ and the Holy Spirit.

Isa.author: Origen of Alexandria
Isa.quote: But you also, who desire to receive the sacred baptism and to merit the grace of the Spirit, ought first to be purged by the law, ought first, having heard the word of God, to cut away your inborn vices and to compose your barbarous and savage ways, so that, having taken up gentleness and humility, you may be able also to receive the grace of the Holy Spirit. For thus says the Lord through the prophet: "Upon whom shall I rest, if not upon the humble and quiet one who trembles at my words?" If you are not "humble and quiet", the grace of the Holy Spirit cannot dwell in you, if you have not received the divine words with trembling. For the Holy Spirit flees from a proud and stubborn and feigning soul. You ought, therefore, first to meditate on the law of God, so that, if perchance your acts are unrestrained and your ways disordered, the law of God may amend and correct you.

Isa.author: Origen of Alexandria
Isa.quote: So long as "King Uzziah" lived, the prophet Isaiah could not "see the vision". For "Uzziah" was a sinner, "doing what was wicked before the sight of the Lord", and acting against the will of the divine law. "He entered the temple" and the holy of holies, and for this reason he was covered with "leprosy on his forehead", so that, going outside the city, he was reckoned among the unclean. Such a ruler of the soul, therefore, must die, that we may be able "to see the vision" of God; for not in vain is it written: "and it came to pass in the year in which King Uzziah died, I saw the Lord". For each one of us "Uzziah" is alive, or Pharaoh, and we do not "groan" while doing the "works" of Egypt. But if he "dies", then we "groan", as it is written in Exodus. If "Uzziah" lives, we do not "see the glory of God"; but if he "dies", then we "see"—as soon as "Uzziah dies"—"the glory of God", provided only that the Word "reign" in us, the Word who said: "but I have been appointed king by him", and that wrath does not "reign". Indeed there is also a "king" of "sin"; the Apostle, knowing this, says: "let sin therefore not reign in your mortal body". Wretched is that man in whom "sin reigns", who hands himself over to such a "king", despising the kingdom of God and subjecting himself to pleasure. Therefore the lover of pleasure is not a lover of God, and according to the Apostle it is said of certain persons: "loving pleasure more than God". And indeed this very thing was said not of those who are entirely unbelievers, but of those who dwell within, "loving pleasure more than God, having a semblance of piety but denying its power". These things are said on account of the death of "King Uzziah", after whose demise the prophet says he "saw the vision". But what is the "vision"? "I saw the Lord seated upon a throne lofty and exalted". Not everyone who "sees the Lord" "sees" him "seated upon a throne lofty and exalted". I know that another prophet "saw the Lord" and "saw" him "seated upon a throne", but not "lofty" nor "exalted". Expounding the Scripture, Daniel says: "thrones were placed", and that "throne" was not "lofty". And: "I will come to sit in judgment over the people in the valley of Jehoshaphat". Therefore here he "sat in the valley", and "in the valley" when he is about "to judge", when he is about to condemn. But it is another thing "to see him seated upon a throne lofty and exalted". And in Micah "God goes forth and descends". And in order to see Sodom, "he descends": "Descending", he says, "I will see whether they have carried out to the full according to the cry of them that comes to me". God, therefore, is sometimes seen above, sometimes below, according to the dignity of the matters at hand. "I saw the Lord", then, Isaiah says, "seated upon a throne lofty and exalted". If I "see God" reigning over those who are here, I do not "see" him "upon a throne lofty and exalted"; if I "see" him "reigning" over the heavenly powers, I "see" him "upon a throne lofty and exalted". What do I mean by the heavenly powers? "Thrones, dominions, principalities, powers" are the heavenly powers. And if I "see" him, how he "reigns" over these in the Word, "I saw the Lord seated upon a throne lofty and exalted". "And the house was full of his glory". On high, where his "throne" is "exalted", "the house is also full of his glory". I do not think that this house which is on earth "is full of glory". "The Lord's is the earth and the fullness thereof". But the "fullness of the glory of God" you will not find in the present; yet if anyone builds a temple to God, the "glory of God" will be seen, and if he keeps what has been said, "the house" will be seen to be "full of the glory of God". But I do not know whether the "house" is filled with "glory" in this way. And in Leviticus, insofar as concerns the present, not yet—but, God granting, it will be read in the assembly that follows—it is said that the Lord commanded certain things to be done, that the "glory of the Lord" might be seen. Nor will the "glory of God" ever appear if these things are not done. And we shall come to know those things when they have been read.

Isa.author: Origen of Alexandria
Isa.quote: "It came to pass", he says, "in the year in which King Uzziah died, I saw the Lord of Sabaoth sitting upon a throne high and lifted up". The "vision" is recorded; why is the time of the king signified? Give heed to when the "vision" arose: when "King Uzziah died", Isaiah "saw the Lord of Sabaoth sitting upon a throne high and lifted up". If any of us knows who "Uzziah" was and what he did, he can know what the prophet taught through the Spirit, what the divine word sets forth for us. I will go to the life of "King Uzziah" and inquire from the books of Kingdoms and from the history of Chronicles concerning "Uzziah", and there I see that it is necessary, if it is to come to pass that "I should see the Lord of Sabaoth sitting upon a throne high and lifted up", that "King Uzziah" must "die" for me. This "Uzziah", descending from the seed of David and "reigning" over the people of Judah, as long indeed as "Zechariah, who had understanding" lived — for so it is written in the second book of Chronicles — "did what was right in the sight of the Lord". And not content with this, he made great lights for the Lord and set the temple of God in order, and many were his virtues in religion. But when "Zechariah who had understanding" died, then he did evil. Do you wish to know this evil that he did? He was a king, not a priest (one is the royal order, another the priestly order); he wished to "enter into the temple" and to perform the place of a priest and to do a work which had not been granted to him; he "entered in", forestalling the priests, and took the "vessel of libation". But there entered also the "chief of the priests" who was at that time, "and eighty priests with him"; "the chief of the priests said to him": are you not Uzziah, and not a priest? He violently persisted, "and leprosy went up upon his forehead"; he was cast out as dead, he "went out" of the temple, the Lord led him out. Therefore he became a "leper" because of his transgression of the law. Each one is under a kingdom, whether of "sin" or of righteousness. If "sin reigns" in me, I am one of the kings of Israel who "entered the temple" violently; if I am righteous according to the measure of my progress and do what is right and persevere before the sight of God, righteousness "reigns" in me. But as long as the "leper" lived, Isaiah had "unclean lips"; as long as the wicked man lived, Isaiah could not "see the Lord of Sabaoth" and had "unclean lips"; for he was under a wicked king. But when does he begin to "see the vision" of God? "In the year in which Uzziah died". Things similar to these you will be able to learn also from many scriptures, God granting it. In Exodus something of this kind is written: "and it came to pass after many days, the king of Egypt died, and the children of Israel groaned, and their cry went up to God". As long as Pharaoh lived, the "children of Israel" did "not groan", and, placed under punishments, they did not even have the free faculty of "groaning"; for the king was alive, who commanded them to make "bricks and straw". As long as Pharaoh lived, they did "not groan to God"; when Pharaoh died, then they had the strength to lift up their faces wet with weeping. The wicked king lives in our breast as long as Pharaoh the devil lives. Then we labor at "bricks" and "straw", then we swallow our tears in silence and do the first works of iniquity; but when he has died, at the visitation of the Lord our God, then we "groan to the Lord". Therefore let us pray that the kingdom of "sin, which is in our mortal body", may die. For it says: "sin was dead, but I lived"; and again: "sin revived, but I died". When "Uzziah", who holds the kingdom of "sin", "dies", Pharaoh too "dies". When the most wicked "king dies", I lift my eyes to heaven and God hears my voice, as he did for Abraham and Isaac and Jacob; and "I see the Lord of Sabaoth sitting" and reigning "upon a high throne", whom the people did not see; for "Uzziah had not yet died". I wish to insert something similar concerning the good thing, which is contrary to this. This very "Uzziah", as long as "Zechariah who had understanding" lived, "did not sin in the sight of God"; when Zechariah died he turned aside from the Lord, at the time when he was ruling over the people and governing the city. And, reading these things by day and by night and hearing the Lord say: "you ought to have put the money on the table, and I at my coming would have exacted it with interest", let us not gather up "in a napkin the mina" entrusted to us, nor let us "put the money on the table", but let us lend it out to the peoples. And when we have entrusted the Lord's account to you, it will have to be seen how you will pay back what was entrusted "with interest". Amen!

Isa.author: Origen of Alexandria
Isa.quote:
But what is the cause that the one hearing "does not understand and the one seeing does not see"? "The heart of this people", he says, "has been thickened". Since indeed this too must be understood, whence it comes, bodily and spiritual fatness are not the same, nor are bodily and spiritual thinness the same. For that which is bodily thick comes to be in the flesh, and a "fleshly heart" does me no harm if "it be thickened", nor does it profit if by illness or by whatever cause it be made thin. And I suppose that the fleshly "heart" of those who are held by fear becomes such. For as they waste away entirely from sickness, so they say that the thickness too, and whatever is fat about their "heart", is thinned out. What harm, then, does it do me if my bodily "heart" "be thickened"? And suppose too my "heart" be made thin — what profit do I have from that? But by a shared term with the bodily "heart", the ruling part of our soul is named, as is manifest from what is said in the Gospel: "blessed are the clean of heart"; for those are not "clean of heart" who have not within them blood or any bodily matter. But it was said: "blessed are the clean of heart" in the sense of "blessed" are those who have "a clean heart", the ruling part of the soul being named instead of "heart". Since, therefore, the ruling part of our soul, which is said to be in the bodily "heart", is either "clean" or unclean — and our "heart" is unclean indeed when "the worst thoughts go forth from" it, "murders, adulteries, thefts, false witness, blasphemies", but "clean" when there are holy thoughts and divine understandings and a pure mind — on this account it must be judged that it is said to be made thin by the "thin" and holy Spirit of him who is saved, but "thickened" by malice and choked in him who sins. For it is said of the "Holy Spirit", who is according to "wisdom", that he is "only-begotten, manifold, thin, mobile", and that the just man receives this "subtle spirit"; for this "spirit" differs from "all intellectual, clean, subtle spirits". The ruling part of the heart, therefore, is "thin" indeed insofar as it is spiritual, but fat insofar as it is concreted from the vice of bodily matter, full of bodily thoughts, which are under reproach. Thus it is said: "the heart of this people has been thickened". Understand: from this "the heart has been thickened", that there is nothing in it besides human and fleshly cares; for just as the matter of the body is fat, in the same way also are bodily understandings and thoughts. Wherefore, since two things are set before us — that the "heart is thickened" from worldly cares and made thin from spiritual solicitude, when one thinks of the things which are the Lord's, casting off the fatness from the "heart" and knowing that, if his "heart be thickened", he will neither receive the words of God nor see the sacrament of salvation — let us lay aside the thickness and take up that thinness which has been spoken of, so that we too may say, as the prophet: "my soul has thirsted for you; how manifoldly does my flesh thirst for you, in a land desert and pathless and waterless, so in the holy place have I appeared to you" — not as though I were "holy" by nature, but if the prudence "of the flesh" wastes away, and if the prudence "of the flesh" has been wasted, then "in the holy place I shall appear to you". These things in explanation of that which was said: "for the heart of this people has been thickened".

There follows: "and with their ears they have heard heavily". It does me no harm if I "hear heavily" bodily, nor does this become for me a cause that I should not hear the words of God. For just as bodily blindness does me no harm, if my soul has not been blinded, so neither does lightness nor heaviness of bodily hearing hinder me. But there is a certain heaviness of hearing which harms the soul of man. What is this heaviness which is in the hearing of the soul? Sin, according to the scriptures, is "heavy". On which account someone, perceiving his sins, says: "like a heavy burden they have been made heavy upon me". And because "iniquity" is heavy, on this account "it sits upon a talent of lead", as is written in Zechariah. But the Egyptians "were sunk like lead in the mighty water" not because they had "heavy" bodies, but because their souls "had been made heavy" by the "talent of lead upon which iniquity was sitting" — on this account "they were sunk like lead in the mighty water". The heaviness of "the ears", therefore, comes from sin, and the lightness from righteousness. What is it that makes the hearing "hear" not "heavily", but lightly? The "wings" of the Word, the "wings" of virtue; for indeed the "wings" of the Word bestow much lightness. "Who will give me wings like a dove's, and I shall find rest?" This the prophet says, praying not that he may receive the bodily "wings of a dove", but the "wings of the dove" of the Holy Spirit. And again Solomon says of the rich man: "but he equips for himself wings like an eagle, and he turns back into the house of him who presides over him". If, therefore, we take "wings", we shall hear lightly; but if we sin and are negligent about our wings and our "wings" fall away, we shall be "made heavy" and "shall hear heavily". "With their ears", therefore, the sinners "have heard heavily". All the Jews indeed who then "heard" the Savior "heard" him "heavily", and therefore did not believe. And down to this day, as many as, "hearing" the scriptures, have not "heard" the spiritual word, which is light, but the "letter", which is "heavy" and "kills", "hear heavily". And thus Scripture is heard in a twofold manner: by him who does not understand what is said, it is "heard heavily"; but by him who understands it, it is not only not "heard heavily", but rather keenly, whence one becomes an understanding hearer.

And yet another thing is prophesied about the people of the Jews and about all of us, if we sin. "And they have closed their eyes, lest at any time they see with their eyes and hear with their ears and understand with their heart". Of those who do not "see", some are "blind" and on account of blindness do not "see"; some are "in darkness" and therefore do not "see"; but others are neither "in darkness" nor blind, but because they "close their eyes" they do not "see". And the divine Scripture knows these differences, which belong to the ruling part of our heart; for the Savior says "to those who are in bonds: come forth, and to those in darkness, that it may be revealed to them", and "to those sitting in the region and shadow of death: a light has arisen for them". These did not "see" for the reason that they were "in darkness", until "a light should arise for them". "Deaf ones, hear, and blind ones, look". These formerly did not "see" for the reason that they were "blind" by nature. But those who are outside these, and who, in comparison with "the blind" and those who are "in darkness", are much worse, are those who do not "see" for the reason that they have willingly "closed their eyes". And that this is so, as we have asserted, the Savior will be a witness to me, saying: "if you were blind, you would not have sin; but now you say that you see; your sin remains". And he says well: "you say that you see"; for truly "they say that they see" and have the possibility of "seeing", but, "closing their eyes", they do not "see". And if ever you see a soul ingenious for understanding, and swift and eager, that does not meditate on the words of God, know that it is not on account of blindness that it does not "see" those things which are contained in the scriptures, not because it is "in darkness", but because it "closes its eyes". If, therefore, you have heard Scripture saying to those who "close their eyes": "open your eyes and see rightly", "open your eyes from that which you had closed", then you will be able to "see rightly" and to consider the light of truth. And it accuses indeed those about whom the inquiry is made, why they "close their eyes, lest they see"; yet it does not also say this, that it is never expedient to "close" the "eyes" of the soul. For it is expedient, as Isaiah makes plain, saying in what follows: "who will announce to you the eternal place? He who walks in righteousness and speaks the true and right way, stopping his ears, that he may not hear the judgment of blood, closing his eyes, that he may not see iniquity". If it is going to happen that, opening the "eyes" of my soul, I "hear" and perceive base speech, it is better to "close" the entrances than to "hear" and understand things that harm. When, then, do I "close"? When evil things are spoken, so that I may not even understand them. When the words of God are to be seen, then "we turn back and" God "heals" us, sending the word which "heals" those who wish to be cured in Christ Jesus, "to whom is glory and dominion unto the ages of ages. Amen!"

Isa.author: Origen of Alexandria
Isa.quote: Let us examine what this means, which is said: "for the heart of this people has been made fat". Everyone who is occupied in the cares of the present life has "a heart made fat"; for those who dwell among worldly things the "heart is made fat" no otherwise than as if they were being choked by thorns. For this reason the "heart" grows fat and cannot receive the notions of the more subtle spirit. Let us therefore flee from such cares, so that our heart, made thin, may become acceptable to God. Let us flee earthly business; for these are the things by which the "heart is made fat". On account of this the discourse of Moses was subtle (as is written of him in Exodus), because he said that whoever, on account of such subtlety, shall be "pure in heart, they shall see God". For by such eyes God is seen. There are three things that are said: "for the heart of this people has been made fat" and "with their ears they have heard heavily" and "they have closed their eyes". But the things said in this passage can also be understood otherwise, more plainly. For many people think, when they look upon the creatures and contemplate this world, that they see them. And why do I speak of people? Behold, the birds and the four-footed beasts see the sun and the moon and the whole heaven together with the choir of stars, but they do not understand their reasons; only the just and holy, comprehending them through the reason of the wisdom of God, look upon them. Therefore in the eighth Psalm David says: "for I shall see your heavens, the works of your fingers, the moon and the stars, which you have founded". For does the prophet not now "see the heaven and the moon"? But this, that he says: "I shall see", if we consider it, we shall be able to understand.

Isa.author: Origen of Alexandria
Isa.quote: "And the Seraphim stood round about him, six wings to the one, and six wings to the other". I see two "Seraphim", each of them having in itself "six wings". Then the arrangement of the "wings". "And with two wings indeed they covered the face"—not their own, but God's—"and with two wings they covered the feet"—not their own, but God's—"and with two wings they were flying". According to what is written, it seems contradictory: if they "stood", they could not "fly". But it is written: "they stood round about him, six wings to the one and six wings to the other; and with two they covered the face and with two they covered the feet, and with two they were flying; and they cried one to another". Truly these "Seraphim", who are around God, who by knowledge alone say: "Holy, Holy, Holy!", on this account keep the mystery of the Trinity, because they too are holy; for among all the things that are, nothing is holier than these. And not lightly do they say "one to another": "Holy, Holy, Holy!", but they proclaim with a cry the confession that is salutary for all. What are these two "Seraphim"? My Lord Jesus and the Holy Spirit. And do not think that the nature of the Trinity is divided, if the functions of the names are preserved. "They covered the face" of God; for the beginning of God is unknown. But also the "feet"; for what last thing is comprehended in our God? Only the middle things are seen; what was before these, I do not know. From the things that are, I understand God; what will come after these, insofar as they are to come, I do not know. "Who has declared it to him?" said Ecclesiastes. "Announce to me the first things and the last things that shall be, and I will say that you are gods", said Isaiah. From which, if anyone should tell the "past things" and be able to tell the "last things", he is "God"; who, then, can tell them except the "Seraphim"? Who can say: "Holy, Holy, Holy!" except the "Seraphim"? But they laid bare which part of God, so to speak—his middle—and "they cried one to the other", standing beside God "and saying": "Holy, Holy, Holy!". They "stand", therefore, and are moved; they "stand" with God, they are moved in making God known; for understand that "they cover the face, they cover the feet"—they do not move the things that are covered, they do not "cover" the things with which "they fly". And they say: "Holy, Holy, Holy is the Lord of Sabaoth, the whole earth is full of his glory". The coming of my Lord Jesus Christ is announced; and so now "the whole earth is full of his glory". Or else it is not yet "full", but it is to come to pass that it be filled, when that prayer shall have been fulfilled by which the Lord himself commanded us to "pray" to the "Father", saying: "when you pray, say: Our Father, who art in heaven, hallowed be thy name! Thy kingdom come! Thy will be done, as in heaven so on earth!". As yet the "will" of the "Father" is "in heaven"; "on earth" his "will" is not yet fulfilled; and Jesus himself, according to the dispensation of the flesh which he had put on, says: "he gave me all power, as in heaven so on earth"—not that he did not have "power on earth", he who had it "in heaven", and that he received something of the world, he who "had come into his own", but that God might so be believed "on earth" as he was believed "in heaven"; therefore the man Christ received "power" which before he did not have, and up to the present he does not yet have "power" over all "on earth". For over those who sin he does not yet reign; but when the "power" over these too has been given to him, when "all things have been made subject" to him, then the "power" will be complete and he will go about "subjecting all things to himself". But some do not yet wish to be "made subject" to him, but as yet are "subjected" to his enemies. Let us, moreover, say: "shall not my soul be made subject to God? for from him is my salvation".

Isa.author: Origen of Alexandria
Isa.quote: It is impossible to find the beginning of God. The beginning of God's movement you can nowhere grasp—not you, I say, and not anyone else, nor any other of the things that have subsistence. The Savior alone and the Holy Spirit, who have always been with God, see His "face"; and perhaps also the "angels", who "continually see the face of the Father who is in heaven", see also the beginnings of His works. And so too before men "the Seraphim hide their feet"; for the "last things", such as they are, cannot be recounted. "Who has announced concerning the last things?" says the Scripture. The things that we see—granting even that we do see something—are the middle things. What existed before the world we do not know; yet certain things did exist before the world. What is to follow after the world we do not apprehend for certain; yet other things will be after the world. Those things, therefore, that are written—"in the beginning God made heaven and earth. But the earth was invisible and unformed, and darkness was over the abyss; and the Spirit of God was borne over the waters"—these are apprehended; those "waters", over which the "Spirit of God" brooded, belonged to the world. But also the "darkness", which "was over the abyss", is not unbegotten; for both were created out of nothing. Hear God saying in Isaiah: "I am God, who framed light and made darkness". Hear wisdom proclaiming in Proverbs: "before all the abysses I was born". These were not unbegotten; but when or how they were born, I do not know. For by the "Seraphim" are "veiled" the first of God's works, that is, the "face of God"; and likewise also the "feet". The things that after the last age are to be for ages of ages, who can expound? It belongs to garrulous men to promise knowledge of these things—men who do not know that a human being can grasp only those things that are the middle things. And the things that after the world, up to the consummation, are to be in the judgment—concerning the punishments, concerning the recompense—of these too many things are hidden from us. This is because of what is written: "with two they veiled the face". But not only did they "veil", they also "covered over", that is, "veiled", so that neither might even a little of the first things be seen—I mean of the "face"—nor might even a little of the "last things" be recognized, that is, of His "feet". "And with two they were flying". The middle things are laid open for contemplation.

Isa.author: Origen of Alexandria
Isa.quote: My Hebrew master used to say that the two seraphim, which are described in Isaiah as having six wings each and as crying one to another and saying, "Holy, holy, holy is the Lord of hosts," were to be understood to mean the only-begotten Son of God and the Holy Spirit.

Isa.author: Origen of Alexandria
Isa.quote: My Hebrew teacher also used to teach as follows, that since the beginning or the end of all things could not be comprehended by any except our Lord Jesus Christ and the Holy Spirit, this was the reason why Isaiah spoke of there being in the vision that appeared to him two seraphim only, who with two wings cover the face of God, with two cover his feet and with two fly, crying one to another and saying, "Holy, holy, holy is the Lord of hosts; the whole earth is full of your glory." For because the two seraphim alone have their wings over the face of God and over his feet, we may venture to declare that neither the armies of the holy angels, nor the holy thrones, nor the dominions, nor principalities nor powers can wholly know the beginnings of all things and the ends of the universe.

Isa.author: Origen of Alexandria
Isa.quote:
"And they cried out one to another", not "one" to many, but "one to another". For to hear the holiness of God, which is announced by the Savior, according to the dignity of the matter no one can except the Holy Spirit; just as, in turn, to indwell the sanctity of God, which is announced by the Holy Spirit, no one can except the Savior alone. On this account "they cried out one to another and said: Holy, Holy, Holy!" It does not suffice for them to cry 'Holy!' once, nor twice, but they take up the perfect number of the Trinity, that they may manifest the multitude of the holiness of God, which is the repeated commonalty of a threefold holiness; to the holiness of the Father is joined the holiness of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. "For both He who sanctifies and those who are sanctified are all of one". He who "sanctifies" is the Savior, according to this—that as a man He receives holiness from God the Father. And so they say: "Holy, Holy, Holy is the Lord of Sabaoth!". And "Sabaoth" is interpreted, as Aquila has handed down, the Lord of armies.

"The whole earth is full of His glory". Once the "house" was full of "glory", but now to those who are upon the "earth" it is prophesied by the Seraphim that it shall come to pass that Christ will fill "the whole earth" with the "glory" of God. For in all who by their manner of life glorify God, there is "His glory", and thus "the whole earth is full of the glory" of God. Once "the whole earth was" not "full of the glory" of God, but one corner of the earth, when it was said: "God is known in Judea, in Israel His name is great". Glory be to God, "who sent His Son", that "the whole earth might become full of His glory". But what does it profit you if the "earth" is "full" of the "glory" of God because of the churches of the blessed who are everywhere, but you yourself are not a partaker of the "glory" of the "fullness of God"? You too, therefore, labor and strive in all things, seeking the "glory" of God, that it may dwell and find a place also in you, and that you too may become, together with "the whole earth" in which is the "glory" of God, "full of His glory". How does the fullness of the "glory" of God come about through each one of us? If the things I do, the things I speak, are done unto the "glory" of God, then my word and my act become "full" of the "glory" of God. If both my going out and my coming in are unto the "glory" of God, if my food, if my drink, if "all" that I do "is done unto the glory of God", then I too am a partaker of this saying: "the earth is full of His glory".

Isa.author: Origen of Alexandria
Isa.quote: "And with two they were flying, and they said one to another: Holy, Holy, Holy is the Lord of Sabaoth, the whole earth is full of his glory. And the lintel was lifted up by the voice with which they cried", by the "voice" of Jesus Christ and the "voice" of the Holy Spirit. If any one of us hears the "voice" of Jesus Christ and of the Holy Spirit "crying out", the "lintel is lifted up" and becomes higher than at that time when "it was lifted up" and when it was said: "lift up the gates, your princes, and be lifted up, everlasting gates, and the king of glory shall enter in". "And the house was filled with smoke". From the remission of the fire the whole "house was filled". And "smoke" is the vapor of fire.

Isa.author: Origen of Alexandria
Isa.quote: When therefore I have done all these things, "the lintel was lifted up by the voice with which they cried out". It is a blessed thing, then, for each one of us so to labor that he may become a partaker of the door and of the "lintel" of the door, which is according to the understanding of Christ God. For it is not, I think, unseemly to say that the flesh is called the door and the Word the "lintel". "The lintel was lifted up by the voice with which they cried out, and the house was filled with smoke", with that good "smoke" from the "glory" of God.

Isa.author: Origen of Alexandria
Isa.quote: "And I said: O wretched me, for I am pierced with remorse, since, although I am a man and have unclean lips". I cannot suppose that Isaiah humbled himself; rather, the Scripture says and gives testimony that his "lips are cleansed" by "one of the Seraphim", who "was sent" to "take away his sins". And "one" of the "Seraphim" is my Lord Jesus Christ, who was sent by the Father to "take away" our "sins", and he says: "behold, I have taken away your iniquities and have cleansed away your sins". And do not think it an affront to his nature, if the Son is sent by the Father. Indeed, that you may recognize the unity of the deity in the Trinity, Christ alone in the present reading now forgives "sins", and yet it is certain that "sins" are forgiven by the Trinity. For he who has believed in one, believes in all. Let there be brought to me, then, from the heavenly altar the "tongs", that it may touch my lips. If the "tongs" of the Lord touch "my lips", it "cleanses" them. And if it "cleanses" them and "cuts away" their vices, as we said just now, I shall open my mouth to the Word of God, and no longer shall an "unclean" word go forth from my mouth, "since, although I am a man and have unclean lips, I also dwell in the midst of a people that has unclean lips". The "Seraphim" that was sent cleansed the "lips" of the prophet, but did not "cleanse the lips of the people". For he himself confessed that "he had unclean lips and dwelt in the midst of a people that has unclean lips". But this "Seraphim" that "was sent" did not judge any of the "people" worthy to have "their lips" too "cleansed", and therefore they still act impiously, therefore they still repudiate my Lord Jesus Christ, still curse him with "unclean lips". But I pray that the "Seraphim" may come and "cleanse" my "lips".

Isa.author: Origen of Alexandria
Isa.quote: "And I saw with my eyes the King, the Lord of Sabaoth". Why should we not set forth in the present a certain tradition of the Jews, plausible indeed yet not true, and why should we not find its solution? They say that Isaiah was for this reason sawn asunder by the people, as one transgressing the law and proclaiming things beyond the Scriptures. For the Scripture says: "no one shall see my face and live", but this man says: "I saw the Lord of Sabaoth". Moses, they say, did not "see", and you have "seen"? And for this reason they sawed him and condemned him as impious; for they did not know that "with two wings the Seraphim covered the face of God". "I saw the Lord". If Isaiah "saw the face", Moses also "saw". Moses "saw the back parts", as it is written; nevertheless he "saw the Lord", even though he did not "see" his "face". And so this man too "saw", although he did not "see" the "face". Wrongly, therefore, did they condemn the prophet. "And I saw with my eyes the King, the Lord of Sabaoth; and one of the Seraphim was sent to me". There is not one single coming of my Lord Jesus Christ by which he descended to the earth; he came both to Isaiah and to Moses, and to the "people" he came, and to each one of the prophets he came; and do not you fear: even though he has now been received up, he will come again. But that he came also before his coming in the flesh, receive as witness the one who declares and says: "Jerusalem! Jerusalem! you who kill the prophets and stone those who are sent to you, how often have I wished to gather your children!". "How often have I wished". He does not say: I did not see you except at this coming, but he says: "how often have I wished". And turning himself through each of the prophets, saying, I was Christ, who spoke through the prophets: do not you fear; and now Jesus Christ is sent. He does not lie. "I am with you", he says, "all the days until the consummation of the age". He does not lie. "Where two or three are gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them". Since, therefore, Jesus Christ is at hand and stands beside us, and the high priest is ready and girded to offer to the Father our supplications, let us rise and through him offer sacrifices to the Father. For "he" is "the propitiation for our sins", "to whom is the glory and the dominion unto the ages of ages. Amen!"

Isa.author: Origen of Alexandria
Isa.quote: "And it came to pass in the year in which King Uzziah died, that I saw the Lord sitting upon a throne high and lifted up; and the house was full of his glory. And the Seraphim stood round about him, six wings to the one and six wings to the other; and with two they veiled his face, and with two they veiled his feet, and with two they flew. And they cried one to another and said: Holy, holy, holy is the Lord of Sabaoth, the whole earth is full of his glory", and the rest. But in order that we too may see the "vision" which Isaiah "saw", let us call upon Jesus, who has bestowed eyes upon those who do not see. For even now he can come and bring it about that we may behold with opened eyes the things that have been spoken in the reading of the sacrament; let us promise him that from now on we will no longer make "the body of Christ the body of a harlot", nor do works worthy of mourning. Let each one of us speak these things in his heart to God, and let us pray that his coming may take place even now; for if Jesus does not come, we cannot see these things. I pray that "a Seraph may be sent to me too", and that, "taking a coal with the tongs, he may cleanse my lips"; and why do I say "lips"? Isaiah was holy, and therefore only his "lips" were "cleansed", because he had offended only with his "lips", that is, in speech. But I am not such that I can say: "I have unclean lips"; I fear that I have an "unclean" heart, "unclean" eyes, "unclean" ears, an "unclean" mouth. As long as I sin in all these, I am wholly "unclean". If "I have looked upon a woman to lust after her, I have committed adultery with her in my heart". Behold, "unclean" eyes. If "out of my breast there go forth evil thoughts, adulteries, fornications, false testimonies", behold, an "unclean" heart. "How beautiful are the feet of those who bring the gospel of peace, who bring the gospel of good things!". But I fear that, running toward evil, I have "unclean feet". "I stretch out" my "hands" to God, and perhaps "turning away his face" he says: "if you stretch out your hands, I will turn my face away from you". Who, then, cleanses me? Who "washes my feet"? Come, Jesus; I have filthy "feet"; for my sake become a servant, "pour your water into your basin", come, "wash my feet". I know that what I say is rash, but I fear the threat of him who says: "if I do not wash your feet, you will have no part with me". Therefore "wash my feet", that "I may have part with you". But why do I say: "wash my feet"? Peter can say this, who had need only that "his feet be washed"; for he was wholly clean. But I, since I have been washed once, need that baptism of which the Lord says: "I have another baptism to be baptized with". Why have we said these things? I am preparing both myself and my hearers for greater mysteries, if indeed the word of God comes, if it descends to us; for I fear that it may flee from me, that it may even disdain to bless me. The word once fled from the people because of "Achar", one sinner; the word fled, I say, from the people because of one sinner, "Achar the son of Zimri, the son of Zerah", from the "tribe of Judah", who was disobedient to God and therefore was "made anathema". And since now there is a multitude of people because of the preparation-day, and especially on the Lord's day, which is the commemoration of Christ's passion — for the resurrection of the Lord is not celebrated once a year, but always after every eighth day — pray to almighty God, that his word may come to us. Even if you are sinners, pray; God hears sinners. But if you fear that which is said in the Gospel: "we know that God does not hear sinners", do not be afraid, do not believe it: he who said this was "blind". Rather believe him who speaks and does not lie: "even if your sins be as scarlet, I will whiten them as wool; and if you are willing and hear me, you shall eat the good things of the earth". If you are "willing" even now to "hear", let us pray in common to the Lord, that at least now, at the coming of the Word, we may be able to give heed to the prophetic sayings.

Isa.author: Origen of Alexandria
Isa.quote: "And I said: O wretched me, for I am pricked with compunction!". Before you "see the vision", do you not confess yourself to be "wretched", O Isaiah? He does not say: so long as "Uzziah" lived did it never come into my mind that I was "wretched"; for I begin to know that I am "wretched" when I "see the vision", when "Uzziah the leprous king" is "dying" for me, and I say: "O wretched me!"? Now I too begin to confess to the Lord and to say of my very self: "O wretched me!", as Isaiah says: "O wretched me!". And close to this the Apostle too says: "wretched man that I am, who shall deliver me from the body of this death?". It is a blessed thing, then, that I should confess myself "wretched". If I humble myself and, repenting, weep over my sins, God will hear me and give me a deliverer, and I say: "thanks be to God through Jesus Christ our Lord!". In truth let us say from the heart: "wretched me". Let each one call to mind the causes of his miseries and his offenses, and let us say, rising to prayer, mindful indeed as though confessing, but forgetful as though no longer committing them, and let us say: "wretched me, for I am pricked with compunction!". He is not "pricked with compunction" before he "saw the vision", before "Uzziah died"; when he begins to do penance, at once he says: "for I am pricked with compunction". If anyone is without feeling "in respect of the inner man", though he be a sinner, he is not "pricked with compunction"; but just as, though you apply a goad to the outer members, the dead body does not feel it, in the same way also, even if you apply the divine words to a sinner who has been put to death through sin and does not do penance, he is neither sorrowful nor repentant, nor has he "the sorrow that works confession, the sorrow that is according to God". But if anyone wishes to be saved and hears the words of one reproving and correcting him, at once he says: "O wretched me". Nor does it suffice to say: "wretched me"; there must be added to it: "because I am pricked with compunction". And would that he might be "pricked with compunction" yet more! For the more we are "pricked with compunction", the more the bonds of our sins are loosed from us. On this account that Ahab gained no great profit, because he was not much "pricked with compunction", but he was indeed "pricked with compunction", yet only once. For which reason it was said: "have you seen how Ahab has been pricked with compunction!" But if anyone be such that he does not cease to be "pricked with compunction", he says likewise as the Apostle: "I am not worthy to be called an Apostle, because I persecuted the Church of God", and: "to me, the least of all the saints, this grace was given", and: "faithful is God, for Jesus Christ came into this world to save sinners, of whom I am the first". Do you see that he was much "pricked with compunction", not once but always—that in writing and speaking and acting he was "pricked with compunction"? As also Isaiah in the present passage, who says: "O wretched me, for I am pricked with compunction, because, since I am a man and have unclean lips, I dwell also in the midst of a people that has unclean lips". Note also another thing: that the sins of Isaiah were not also in deeds, but only in words; for which reason he says: "because, since I am a man and have unclean lips". But there was also "a people having unclean lips"; it did not befit him to accuse the "people" and to say that there were more sins in it than of "unclean lips".

Isa.author: Origen of Alexandria
Isa.quote:
"And I saw with my eyes the King, the Lord of Sabaoth". If ever we have thought about God while we are still sinners, we too say what the prophet now says: "and one of the Seraphim was sent to me". How good is God! Because, He says, I hear Isaiah confessing—for he said: "O wretched me!"—because I hear him repenting—for he says: "I am pricked with compunction"—because he has declared his own offenses, saying: "since I am a man and have unclean lips, I dwell also in the midst of a people having unclean lips", I too, "while he is yet speaking, say: behold, I am present". "And one of the Seraphim was sent to me, and in his hand he had a coal". A "coal" is brought to the prophet, that through the burning of fire his "lips" might be purged, which had at some time sinned. Who is this "one of the Seraphim"? My Lord Jesus Christ: He, according to the dispensation of the flesh, was sent, having in His hand a "coal" and saying: "I came to send fire upon the earth, and would that it were already kindled!"

"And one of the Seraphim was sent to me, and in his hand he had a coal, which he had taken with tongs from the altar". Not by just any "fire" simply and by chance is the prophet purged, but by that which is "from the altar" of God. If you have not been purged by the "fire" of the "altar", there remains for you that fire of which it was said: "depart from me into the eternal fire, which is prepared for the devil and his angels". Not such is the "fire" that is "from the altar". All are to be delivered to the "fire", but not all to one "fire": some the "fire" "from the altar" awaits, others "that" which "is prepared for the devil and his angels".

Isa.author: Origen of Alexandria
Isa.quote: We read also in Isaiah that the prophet is purged by fire through "one of the seraphim, which was sent to him, when it took with tongs one coal from those which were upon the altar, and touched the lips of the prophet and said": "behold, I have taken away your iniquities". To me these things seem to be mystical and to indicate this, that to each one, according to that in which he sins, if he is worthy to be purified, coals are applied to his members. For since the prophet here says: "I have unclean lips, and I dwell also in the midst of a people having unclean lips", therefore the "coal taken up with the tongs" by the seraph purges his lips, in which alone he professes himself not to be clean. From which it is shown that only as far as the word was his sin found, but that in deed or work he had sinned in nothing; otherwise he would have said that I have an unclean body, or I have unclean eyes, if he had sinned in desiring the things of others, and he would have said: I have unclean hands, if he had polluted them with wicked works. But now, since perhaps in speech alone he was conscious to himself of that fault of which the Lord says: "that even for an idle word you shall render account in the day of judgment", because it is difficult even for the perfect to avoid the fault of speech, therefore the prophet too needed only the purging of the lips.

Isa.author: Origen of Alexandria
Isa.quote:
Let the reproving word, therefore, touch the "lips" of our mind and soul, that we too may say: "and it touched my mouth". If I shall have cleansed "my mouth", so that I speak nothing idle, nothing foolish, nothing base, nothing scurrilous—to name them all at once—nothing of those things that are forbidden, then I can say: "it touched my mouth". But so long as I "have unclean lips" and carry on unclean affairs, because of the words of sin "the fire from the altar does not touch me", nor "is one of the Seraphim sent to me".

"And He said: behold, this has touched your lips, and it has taken away your iniquities, and has purged your sins round about". Let the divine word bite us, let it burn up our souls, and let us say as we hear: "was not our heart burning within us?", that "our iniquities and sins may be taken away", and that, made clean, with clean mouth and clean heart and a whole clean conscience, we may give thanks to almighty God in Christ Jesus, "to whom is glory and dominion for ages of ages. Amen!"

Isa.author: Origen of Alexandria
Isa.quote:
Isaiah, "seeing the Lord of Sabaoth seated upon a lofty and lifted-up throne", and "seeing" also "the Seraphim standing about him", and receiving the remission of sins through that fire which, brought "from the altar", "cleansed" his "lips" by its touch, says that "he heard the voice of the Lord" — not commanding, but rousing and "saying": "whom shall I send, and who will go to this people?" Then he says that "he answered" the Lord: "behold, it is I, send me". But when I take my place here and search into what is written, I find that Moses did one thing and Isaiah another. For Moses, chosen for the leading-out of the people from the land of Egypt, says: "provide another whom you may send", and he seems to contradict God; but Isaiah, not chosen, but "hearing": "whom shall I send, and who will go?", says: "behold, it is I, send me". It is worthwhile, therefore, for one "comparing spiritual things with spiritual" to inquire which of the two did better: Moses, who, after he was chosen, refused, or Isaiah, who, without even being chosen, offered himself to be "sent to the people". For I do not know whether anyone, attending to that contrariety of the affairs which appears in each, can say that Moses did the very same thing as Isaiah. So then I boldly make a comparison of these two holy and blessed men, and I decide and declare that Moses acted more modestly than Isaiah. For Moses was considering the magnitude of presiding over the people so as to lead them out of the land of Egypt, of contending against the "incantations" and sorceries of the Egyptians; on this account he says: "provide another whom you may send". But this man, not waiting to hear what would be enjoined upon him to say — even if he had been chosen — says: "behold, it is I, send me". Hence, because, being ignorant of what would be enjoined upon him, he says: "behold, it is I, send me", he is commanded to say those very things which were unwished-for by the one who was to say them. Or was it not undesirable, having been immediately bidden to prophesy, to begin from curses, saying: "with the ear you will hear and not understand, and seeing you will perceive and not see; for the heart of this people has been thickened" and the rest? Perhaps, then — if indeed it is expedient to say it boldly — he received as the wage of his rashness and boldness that he was commanded to say the very things which he was unwilling to prophesy. But since we have compared Isaiah and Moses, let us set up also another comparison closely akin, Isaiah and Jonah. The latter is sent "to preach" the overthrow of the Ninevites after "three days", and it irks him, unwilling to set out, to be the cause of evils for the city. But this man, not waiting for what would be commanded him to say, says: "behold, it is I, send me". It is good not to leap forward toward those dignities and offices of rule and ministries of the Church which are from God; would that we imitated Moses and said with him: "provide another whom you may send". For he who wishes to be saved comes to the rule of the Church not to lordship — even though he presides — but to servitude, if one must speak also from the Gospel: "the princes of the nations indeed lord it over them, and those who have power over them are called magistrates; but it shall not be so among you". For neither do "the princes lord it over you", but "whoever of you wishes to be greater shall be least of all"; "whoever wishes to be first shall be last of all". He, therefore, who is called to the episcopate is called not to lordship, but to the servitude of the whole Church.
